findings.quote: Poor peripheral circulation, cold hands and movement degrade the signal.
findings.explanation: The paragraph on oximeter limits omits skin pigmentation. Pulse oximeters can overestimate saturation in people with darker skin, so a normal reading can falsely reassure (documented by the NHS Race and Health Observatory review, 2022, and the UK Independent Review of Equity in Medical Devices, 2024). Nail varnish and false nails also interfere. Together with the unqualified '95 to 100% is normal' (body[1] and the key fact) and no emergency pointer on the carbon monoxide sentence, a UK reader could be misled; a usual baseline also differs in some chronic lung disease (UK target 88-92% in people at risk of carbon dioxide retention).
findings.suggestedFix: Add skin pigmentation (and nail varnish) to the listed limits, with a source, and say that a normal reading does not exclude low oxygen in someone who is unwell. Add one clause that suspected carbon monoxide poisoning is an emergency. Consider noting that 'normal' differs for some people with chronic lung disease.

findings.quote: Volumes fall with age, height and smoking and rise with training
findings.explanation: Height is listed as something that makes lung volumes fall. The opposite is true: taller people have larger lungs, which is why predicted values are matched to height. The same page says total lung capacity is 'larger ... in tall people than in short' (body[3]) and that predicted values depend on height (body[4]). Minor related point: the same sentence says reference values are matched to 'ethnicity' but body[5] says age, sex and height only; race-neutral reference equations are now recommended by the ATS (2023), so check current UK practice.
findings.suggestedFix: Volumes rise with height and training and fall with age and smoking; reference values are matched to age, sex and height (state the ethnicity point only if it matches current UK laboratory practice).

findings.quote: the anion gap calculated from the panel shows whether the blood is too acidic or not acidic enough
findings.explanation: The anion gap (sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate, with or without potassium) is used to look for unmeasured acids in a metabolic acidosis (raised gap: ketones, lactate, toxins, kidney failure) and to narrow the cause. It cannot show that blood is 'not acidic enough' (alkalosis), and a normal gap does not show that pH is normal; pH comes from a blood gas.
findings.suggestedFix: the anion gap, calculated from the panel, helps identify the cause of a metabolic acidosis.

findings.quote: a rise in carbon dioxide in the alveoli, or a fall in oxygen in the blood supplying them, widens the bronchioles so that carbon dioxide can be cleared faster
findings.explanation: In local ventilation-perfusion matching, high alveolar carbon dioxide dilates the bronchioles, whereas low alveolar oxygen constricts the pulmonary arterioles (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction). Low oxygen is not the standard bronchodilating signal; the clause as written merges the two mechanisms and then says this 'complements' vessel constriction, which makes the logic circular.
findings.suggestedFix: a rise in carbon dioxide in the alveoli widens the bronchioles so that carbon dioxide is cleared faster, while a fall in alveolar oxygen constricts the arterioles supplying them, diverting blood to better-ventilated regions.

findings.quote: Treatment follows the WPATH, Endocrine Society and UCSF guidelines; in England it is started by NHS gender dysphoria clinics, with prescribing and monitoring often shared with the GP.
findings.explanation: On a UK-first page this presents two international professional guidelines and a US clinic's protocol as what governs care. NHS adult gender dysphoria clinics work to an NHS England service specification and GMC prescribing guidance, informed by (not bound to) those documents. The page also never says it describes adult care. NHS England policy for under-18s is different and restrictive (for example puberty blockers are no longer routinely available outside research following the Cass Review) and has been changing, so a young reader or parent could take this as the NHS pathway for them.
findings.suggestedFix: State that the page describes adult hormone treatment. Say that NHS clinics follow NHS England's adult service specification, informed by international guidance (WPATH SOC8, Endocrine Society), and that the timetables below are drawn from Endocrine Society/UCSF tables. Add a line that care for under-18s is different, pointing to the NHS page.

findings.quote: so that every absorbed molecule passes a liver cell before reaching the general circulation
findings.explanation: Not every absorbed molecule goes through the liver first. physiology/absorption body[0] says fats are rebuilt into chylomicrons and enter the lymphatic lacteals, 'bypassing the liver at first'; some drugs absorbed from the mouth or rectum also bypass it. The summary ('processes everything absorbed from the gut') has the same overstatement.
findings.suggestedFix: so that most absorbed nutrients, other than fats carried in lymph, pass a liver cell before reaching the general circulation.

findings.quote: Glial cells outnumber neurons and feed, insulate and protect them.
findings.explanation: The old '10 glia to 1 neuron' figure has been revised. Cell-counting studies (Azevedo 2009, the source of the ~86 billion neuron figure used on this page, and the 2016 review by von Bartheld and colleagues) give roughly one non-neuronal cell per neuron in the whole human brain, with the ratio varying by region (more glia per neuron in cortex, far fewer in the cerebellum).
findings.suggestedFix: Glial cells are about as numerous as neurons and feed, insulate and protect them (or delete the comparison).

findings.quote: with a combined surface close to the size of a tennis court
findings.explanation: A tennis court is about 195 m2 (singles) to 260 m2 (doubles). The page's own key fact gives the exchange surface as about 70 m2, roughly a quarter to a third of a court, so body and key fact disagree.
findings.suggestedFix: with a combined surface of roughly 70 m2 (delete the tennis-court comparison).

findings.quote: The NHS describes finding it on the inside of the wrist at the base of the thumb
findings.explanation: The paragraph attributes the pulse-taking method (site, fingers, counting time, resting conditions) to the NHS, but none of the page's references is an NHS page (OpenStax, British Heart Foundation, NHLBI). The reader cannot trace the attribution, and it is not clear the cited BHF page carries the same detail.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the NHS page on checking your pulse to the references (and verify the details against it), or attribute the method to the cited BHF page if it carries them.

findings.quote: sustained readings of 140/90 mmHg or more define hypertension in most guidelines
findings.explanation: For a UK reader (NICE NG136, NHS) hypertension is diagnosed from clinic readings of 140/90 or more confirmed by a home or ambulatory average of 135/85 or more. body[5] says diagnosis is usually confirmed by home or ambulatory monitoring, but only 140/90 is ever given, so home readings could be compared with the wrong threshold. 'Most guidelines' is also loose: the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline defines hypertension from 130/80.
findings.suggestedFix: In the UK, hypertension is diagnosed when clinic readings are 140/90 mmHg or higher and the average at home or on ambulatory monitoring is 135/85 mmHg or higher.

findings.quote: detected on a basic metabolic panel
findings.explanation: 'Basic/wider metabolic panel' is US terminology, and body[5] likewise describes an 'electrolyte panel' of sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate plus a calculated anion gap. UK laboratories report urea and electrolytes (U&E, 'renal profile') with a separate bone profile for calcium; chloride and an anion gap are not usually reported on a routine UK U&E. US-only practice is presented as general on a UK-first site.
findings.suggestedFix: detected on a urea and electrolytes (U&E) blood test; reword body[5] to describe what UK U&E and bone profile report, or label the US panel as US.

findings.quote: Six ions do most of the work: sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, calcium and phosphate.
findings.explanation: The summary names sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride and bicarbonate (magnesium, no phosphate); this paragraph names a different six (phosphate, no magnesium). Magnesium is then described separately in body[1] and phosphate only in passing in body[4].
findings.suggestedFix: Make summary and body agree (list the same ions in both, or name both phosphate and magnesium).

findings.quote: The voice deepens over the first year and the change is permanent; facial and body hair start to grow within about three to six months and keep increasing for three to five years
findings.explanation: Effects and timings are population-level expectations, but this paragraph and the key facts ('starts at 3-6 months; maximum at 2-3 years', 'deepens within the first year; permanent') state them as definite outcomes, unlike the feminising paragraph ('The guideline timetables give ...'). Response varies between individuals (degree and speed of voice change, hair pattern, fat distribution) and none is guaranteed. Also check the hair and voice timelines against the cited Endocrine Society/UCSF tables: as I recall them they give facial/body hair onset at 6-12 months with maximum at 4-5 years, and voice onset at 6-12 months with maximum at 1-2 years.
findings.suggestedFix: Preface with 'In guideline tables, typically ...' and add 'individual response varies and is not guaranteed'; use the same wording in the key facts; verify the numbers against the cited tables.

findings.quote: while protein or blood in the urine signals that the barrier itself is damaged, as in glomerulonephritis or diabetic kidney disease
findings.explanation: Overgeneralised. Protein and blood in the urine have many non-glomerular causes: urinary infection, stones, tumours of the kidney or bladder, menstrual contamination, and transient proteinuria with fever or exercise. Blood in the urine needs assessment whatever its source, but this sentence points readers only to kidney-filter disease. body[2] ('Protein in the urine means the sieve is damaged.') is similarly categorical.
findings.suggestedFix: protein or blood in the urine can signal that the barrier itself is damaged, as in glomerulonephritis or diabetic kidney disease, but blood can also come from anywhere along the urinary tract and needs assessment.

findings.quote: Its two main roles, in the NIDDK's summary, are making insulin and making the digestive juices that break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats in the intestine.
findings.explanation: Follows 'The exocrine tissue is the bulk of the organ.', so 'Its' reads as the exocrine tissue, which makes digestive juices but not insulin (beta cells of the endocrine islets make insulin). It contradicts the page summary and body[1].
findings.suggestedFix: The pancreas has two main jobs: its exocrine tissue, which is most of the organ, makes digestive juices, and the islets make hormones such as insulin.

findings.quote: which is why a murmur heard between S1 and S2 arises during ejection
findings.explanation: A murmur heard between S1 and S2 is a systolic murmur, but not all systolic murmurs arise during ejection. Ejection murmurs (aortic stenosis, flow murmurs) do, whereas regurgitant murmurs (mitral or tricuspid regurgitation, ventricular septal defect) are holosystolic and start at S1 during isovolumetric contraction, before any ejection. The 'which is why' also does not follow from the valve closures just described.
findings.suggestedFix: a murmur heard between S1 and S2 arises during systole, either from blood ejected through a narrowed or roughened valve or from blood leaking backwards through an incompetent atrioventricular valve.

findings.quote: prolonged exercise or a missed meal does not cause hypoglycaemia in a healthy person
findings.explanation: Stated as an absolute. The glycogen and gluconeogenesis buffer makes hypoglycaemia uncommon in healthy people, but it can happen after very prolonged or intense exercise, prolonged fasting, or with alcohol, so 'does not cause' overstates and could falsely reassure.
findings.suggestedFix: usually prevents hypoglycaemia in a healthy person.

findings.quote: initiates and times movements using information about balance and body position
findings.explanation: The cerebellum does not initiate voluntary movement (motor cortex and basal ganglia do; cerebellar damage causes incoordination and ataxia, not paralysis). It coordinates, times and corrects movement and contributes to balance and motor learning. The same page says 'the cerebellum times and coordinates movement' (body[1]).
findings.suggestedFix: coordinates and times movements using information about balance and body position.

findings.quote: Beta cells make up about three quarters of each islet and release insulin when blood glucose is high; alpha cells make up about a fifth
findings.explanation: The 75%/20% split (repeated in the key facts as 'share of each islet') is the rodent/older textbook figure. Quantitative studies of human islets give roughly 50-60% beta, 30-40% alpha and about 10% delta cells, with wide variation between islets (Brissova 2005; Cabrera 2006). 'Each islet' implies a fixed composition.
findings.suggestedFix: Say that beta cells are the largest group and alpha cells a substantial minority (give human proportions only with a source) and drop 'each'; change the key facts to match.

findings.quote: an absorbing surface roughly six hundred times its outer surface
findings.explanation: Conflicts with body[0] and the key fact (about 30 m2). The outer surface of the small intestine is a fraction of a square metre (a tube 3-6 m long and about 3 cm wide), so a 600-fold gain corresponds to the older estimate of roughly 150-350 m2 (the 'tennis court' figure), not 30 m2. Recent measurements support about 30 m2; the page mixes the two figures.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the '600 times' statement or reconcile it with one sourced figure.

notes: Read all 35 physiology entities (both printer ranges) in full. No web access used; every point is from recall and is graded by the confidence field. All 20 quotes were machine-checked as exact substrings of content/physiology.json at the stated path. The cap of 20 was reached; the next-best points that were left out are: (1) hormones body[4] 'diabetes is the most common endocrine disease in the United States' (US statistic on a UK-first page); (2) fluid-balance summary 'within a litre of its set point' is an unsupported precision, and key fact plasma osmolality 285-295 mOsm/kg is narrower than the usual laboratory range of about 275-295; (3) oxygen-transport key fact haemoglobin 130-170 g/L is laboratory-dependent and not supported by the cited pages; (4) reflexes: body[1] 'damage above the spinal cord' conflicts with body[4]/body[2] (spinal cord injury also gives brisk reflexes), and body[3] 'needing only one sensory fibre ... and one motor neuron' conflicts with body[0] (withdrawal uses an extra interneuron); (5) circulation body[2] coronary supply 'during diastole' is true mainly for the left ventricle, and body[5] 'in shock the skin becomes cool and mottled' is not true of warm (early septic) shock; (6) cardiac-cycle key facts EDV 130 ml and stroke volume 70 ml give an ejection fraction of about 54%, just under the quoted 55-70%, and body[0] says ventricular pressure must exceed aortic pressure for the pulmonary valve too; (7) sensory-systems body[0] 'hair cells fire in proportion to pitch' (pitch is place-coded, firing rate codes intensity); (8) neurons body[5] 'Researchers have identified new neurons forming in the adult human brain' is contested; nerve-signals says 85 billion neurons, neurons says 86 billion; (9) gut-motility body[2] describes bowel obstruction (vomiting, no gas) with no urgent-care pointer, and the 'vomiting lasting more than an hour' advice in body[5] could not be checked; (10) pancreatic-functions body[4] says acute pancreatitis 'usually settles' with no urgent-care pointer, and body[5] 'diabetes mellitus is diagnosed when insulin production fails' conflates cause with diagnosis; (11) co2-removal body[4] 'pH barely moves' in heavy exercise holds for the carbon dioxide effect only (lactic acid does lower pH); (12) cardiac-output body[3] Fick caveat about the lungs' own oxygen use is hard to follow and its direction is unclear. Editorial: endocrine-glands body[2] ('In this atlas ... not part of the dataset') is internal scaffolding text visible to readers; the cardiac-cycle MedlinePlus reference uses host www.medlineplus.gov unlike every other MedlinePlus link. Typical values: most keyFacts ranges are given as fixed facts without a per-fact source or a 'laboratory ranges vary' caveat, and several rest on US textbook (OpenStax) values; a single standard caption would help. Gender-affirming hormones: apart from the two findings listed, the content matches my recollection of the Endocrine Society expected-effects tables for the feminising regimen, the ICD-11 classification statement is correct, the thrombosis warning and screening paragraphs are appropriate, and the trans-inclusive statements on menopause, menstrual-cycle, pregnancy and sex-hormones are neutral and consistent. Omissions to consider rather than errors: body[3] calls venous thromboembolism 'the main risk of oestrogen' and does not mention other monitored risks (cardiovascular disease, gallstones, raised triglycerides, meningioma with cyproterone); the testosterone paragraph does not state that testosterone is harmful in pregnancy, which is the reason its contraception caveat matters. cleanEntities lists only entities with no point at all; entities with only the minor unlisted points above (cardiac-output, circulation, co2-removal, reflexes, sensory-systems, gut-motility, fluid-balance, hormones) are deliberately not listed as clean.
